text: That logo on the part is a layer of ink thinner than a hair.
Here's how it gets there.
Tampo printing. Also called pad printing.
The image is etched into a steel plate, called the cliché.
A sealed ink cup slides across it, filling the etch and wiping the rest clean.
The ink in the etch starts to dry, and turns tacky.
A soft silicone pad presses down and lifts the ink out.
Then it moves over the part and presses again, wrapping the image around curves.
The tacky ink sticks to the part better than to the pad, so it lets go cleanly.
But small changes ruin the print.
Dust and lint on the pad leave holes in the image.
Ink too thick won't release. Too thin, and it blurs.
A worn cup ring or cliché leaves streaks and haze.
And oil or release agent on the part stops the ink from sticking.
Warning signs: faded or broken prints, blurry edges, smudges, and ink that peels in a tape test.
So: clean the pad with tape, and replace it when it's worn or cut.
Check the ink viscosity every shift, and keep the cup sealed.
Inspect the cliché and the cup ring, and keep the fixture tight.
Keep the parts clean, and do a tape test on every batch.
Sharp print. Every time.
